abstract: >
  Biodiversity is under threat from multiple global change drivers including climate warming, atmospheric nitrogen deposition, and land-use change such as grazing regimes.
  Several of these drivers affect biodiversity through the same underlying mechanism, namley community biomass.
  We hyopothesise that by using community biomass as a common curency we can simplify the direct and indirect effects of multiple global change drivers.
  We test this prediction in a replicated field experiment in and alpine and sub-alpine grassland, manipulating three common global change drivers: climate warming, nitrogen deposition, grazing, and mimick grazing by clipping. 
  We found that the three global change drivers affect community biomass and diversity, but the impact depended on the site and the limiting resources.
  The three global change drivers operated indeed on diversity through commuity biomass, but only at the alpine site where the grassland was both temperature and nutrient limited.
  Using environmental affinities to describe change in envrionmental niches of these communities reveiled that warming and nitrogen addition led to communities with higher competitive ability for nutrients and light.
  At the sub-alpine community, warming led to less shade tolerant and moisture communities, while high levels of nitrogen addition led to more acidic conditoins. 
  Overall, our study showed that global change drivers operate through similar mechanisms when resources are limited.
